36.title: The sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31–46)
36.hook: the king says: when you fed the hungry and visited the prisoner, you did it to me
36.howItsDone: Christians put this passage into practice through food banks, prison visiting, hospital chaplaincy and clothing drives, and Catholics count its acts among the corporal works of mercy.

segments.voice: Yesterday, ten bridesmaids waited for a groom who came at midnight, and only five had spare oil. Your line was bring a little extra oil. Did you get one thing ready? Day thirty-six.

This is the last story Jesus tells in Matthew's Gospel before the plot against him begins. A king sits on his throne, and all the nations of the world are gathered in front of him. He separates them, the way a shepherd separates the sheep from the goats. To the ones on his right he says: come in. When I was hungry, you fed me. When I was thirsty, you gave me a drink. I was a stranger, and you took me in. I had no clothes, and you clothed me. I was sick, and you visited me. I was in prison, and you came to me. And the people on his right are baffled. When? When did we ever see you hungry?
screen: `A KING ON A THRONE.` → `I WAS HUNGRY, AND YOU FED ME.` → `WHEN DID WE SEE YOU?`

segments.voice: His answer is the line the whole story hangs on: "Inasmuch as ye have done it unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done it unto me." Here's what makes it strange. Neither group knew. The ones who helped didn't know they were helping him. They thought they were just feeding a hungry man. And the ones on the left, who walked past, ask the very same question: when did we see you hungry and not help? They'd have helped, if they'd known. That's the point. He wasn't recognizable. He had an ordinary face. The list is plain on purpose. Food. Water. A spare room. Clothes. A visit to someone sick. A prison visit. No miracles. Things anyone could do on a Tuesday. Catholic tradition took this list, added burying the dead, and called them the corporal works of mercy, the works of the body. Christian hospitals, food banks and prison ministries often point back to this passage. Who are the least of these? Christians have read it two ways: everyone in need, anywhere, or Jesus's own followers who are poor and suffering. Both readings have their defenders. In both, the king is found in the one who needs help. It's a hard story too. The ones who walked past are sent away, and Matthew doesn't soften it. And with this, the parables end. Fifteen days of stories: seeds and yeast, a lost sheep, a lost coin, a pearl, workers paid too much, buried talents, bigger barns, a servant who wouldn't forgive, two men praying, a widow knocking, an empty banquet, a flask of oil. And last, a king with an ordinary face.
screen: `NEITHER GROUP KNEW` · `A LIST ANYONE CAN DO` · `WHO ARE THE LEAST OF THESE?` · `THE LAST OF THE PARABLES` · then, large: `YE HAVE DONE IT UNTO ME.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Go down the king's list slowly, one breath each. Hungry. Thirsty. A stranger. Without enough to wear. Sick. In prison. With each one, let a face come, if one does. Someone real. Someone you've walked past, or someone you know. Then choose one: someone you could feed, visit or clothe this week. A meal dropped off. A visit to someone who's ill. A coat you don't wear, given to someone who needs it. Hold that plan, and sit. The bell holds the time.
The sheep and the goats. A king who says: whatever you did for the least, you did for me. The last of the parables.
screen: `THE SHEEP AND THE GOATS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: he wears ordinary faces. This week, feed, visit or clothe one person. Tomorrow the parables are behind us, and the stories go back to the beginning: a small town called Nazareth, and a young woman named Mary. Day thirty-six.

37.title: The angel in Nazareth (Luke 1:26–38)
37.hook: Gabriel greets a young woman in a small town, and she asks one honest question before saying yes
37.howItsDone: Churches keep the Annunciation as a feast on March 25; Catholics pray the Hail Mary and the Angelus, which retell this scene, Orthodox Christians sing hymns to Mary as Theotokos, and Protestant churches often read the passage in Advent.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last parable: a king who said, whatever you did for the least, you did for me. Your line was he wears ordinary faces. Did you see one? Day thirty-seven. The parables are done. Today a new week begins, in Nazareth.
screen: `HE WEARS ORDINARY FACES.` → `WEEK SIX: MARY AND NAZARETH.`

segments.voice: A small town in the hills of Galilee. Nazareth. So small and so ordinary that later in the Gospels someone asks whether anything good could come out of it. A young woman named Mary lives there. She's engaged to a man called Joseph. And one day, Luke says, the angel Gabriel comes in to where she is and greets her: hail, you who are highly favored, the Lord is with you. Mary is troubled. Luke says she turned the words over in her mind, wondering what kind of greeting this could be. The angel says: don't be afraid. You're going to have a son, and you'll name him Jesus. And Mary doesn't faint, and doesn't simply nod. She asks one question.
screen: `NAZARETH. A SMALL TOWN.` → `AN ANGEL'S GREETING.` → `SHE ASKS ONE QUESTION.`

segments.voice: Her question is practical: "How shall this be, seeing I know not a man?" She's engaged, not married. Luke tells the answer plainly: the Holy Spirit will come upon her, and the child will be called the Son of God. And her older relative Elizabeth, the one people called barren, is six months pregnant. "For with God nothing shall be impossible." Then Mary answers, and this is the line the week turns on: "Behold the handmaid of the Lord; be it unto me according to thy word." A question, and then a yes. Not a yes without thinking. A yes after thinking. Luke never gives her age. Some readers picture a teenager, but the text doesn't say. This scene has a name: the annunciation, the announcement. Tradition keeps its feast on March twenty-fifth, nine months before Christmas. Gabriel's first word in Greek is an everyday greeting that literally means rejoice. The next words, highly favored, are one Greek word, which the old Latin Bible rendered full of grace. Christians honor Mary in different ways, and this scene runs through them. Catholics pray the Hail Mary, which begins with Gabriel's greeting. Orthodox Christians call her the Theotokos, the God-bearer, and sing to her often. Protestants often honor her above all as a model of faith: someone who heard something impossible, asked her honest question, and said yes.
screen: `AN HONEST, PRACTICAL QUESTION` · `A YES AFTER THINKING` · `REJOICE, FULL OF GRACE` · `ONE MARY, HONORED MANY WAYS` · then, large: `BE IT UNTO ME ACCORDING TO THY WORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Think of one small thing you've been hesitating over. Not a life decision. A small one. A call you keep not making. An invitation you haven't answered. A favor someone asked for. Breathe. Now do what Mary does in the story: ask your honest question first. What's the worry, really? Let it be said, inside. Then, if it still seems good, say yes to it. Quietly. One small yes for today. Then sit. The bell holds the time.
Annunciation. The announcement: an angel, a young woman's question, and her yes. Today's word.
Your line: be it unto me. Once today, when something good but inconvenient comes along, ask your question, and then say yes. Day thirty-seven.

38.title: Two pregnant women (Luke 1:39–45)
38.hook: Mary hurries to her cousin Elizabeth, and the baby in Elizabeth's womb leaps
38.howItsDone: Many churches keep the Feast of the Visitation (May 31 in the Catholic calendar). Catholics say Elizabeth's greeting every time they pray the Hail Mary; Christian art often paints the two women embracing at the door.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the annunciation. An angel in Nazareth, one honest question, and a yes. Your line was: be it unto me. What small thing did you say yes to? Day thirty-eight.

Some news needs one person who'll just get it. Not advice. Just understanding. Mary has one. The angel mentioned her: Elizabeth, her older relative, married to a priest called Zacharias, the woman everyone had written off as unable to have children, now six months pregnant. So Luke says Mary gets up and goes with haste, into the hill country of Judah, a long way south of Nazareth. A young woman with news she can't explain to anyone at home, walking to the one house where someone might understand. She reaches the door. She calls out a greeting. And before she can say another word, something happens inside Elizabeth.
screen: `THE ONE WHO'D JUST GET IT.` → `WITH HASTE, INTO THE HILLS.` → `A GREETING AT THE DOOR.`

segments.voice: Luke says it in the King James Bible like this: when Elizabeth heard Mary's greeting, "the babe leaped in her womb." And Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, cries out with a loud voice: "Blessed art thou among women, and blessed is the fruit of thy womb." Notice what hasn't happened. Mary hasn't told her anything. There's no explaining, no convincing, no awkward conversation. Elizabeth already knows. Then she asks a question that sounds almost embarrassed: "And whence is this to me, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?" Who am I, that you'd come to me? The older woman, the priest's wife, honoring the young woman from the small town. Then she tells Mary what happened: as soon as your greeting reached my ears, "the babe leaped in my womb for joy." That baby will grow up to be John the Baptist, the wild man by the river we'll meet in a few weeks. Some readers see this as the first time anyone in Luke recognizes Jesus, and it's a child who hasn't been born yet, leaping. Joy recognizing joy. And Elizabeth ends with a blessing, not for the baby this time, but for Mary herself: "blessed is she that believed." This visit is called the Visitation, and it has its own feast day in the Western church calendar. Elizabeth's words later joined Gabriel's greeting in the Hail Mary, the prayer Catholics say, and in the Orthodox hymn to Mary that begins with the angel's rejoice. Luke adds a small detail at the end of the chapter. Mary stays about three months. Two women, one old and one young, both carrying something they didn't expect, keeping each other company until the time comes.
screen: `THE BABE LEAPED IN HER WOMB.` · `SHE KNEW BEFORE SHE WAS TOLD.` · `WHO AM I, THAT YOU'D COME TO ME?` · `THREE MONTHS TOGETHER.` · then, large: `JOY KNOWS JOY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your shoulders drop. Think of the person who'd understand. Not fix it, just understand. Someone who's been through something like what you're carrying, or who simply knows you well enough that you wouldn't need to explain. Hold their face for a few breaths. Notice what it feels like to be known without explaining. If you pray, you can hold them in your prayer. If you don't, just let yourself be glad they exist. Then, if you can, choose a time today to visit them, or call. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Two pregnant women. Mary and Elizabeth, the young one and the old one, and a baby who leaped for joy before a word was explained.
Your line: joy knows joy. Visit or call someone who'll understand, today. No need to explain much. Day thirty-eight.

39.title: Mary's song (Luke 1:46–55)
39.hook: she sings of a God who lifts the lowly and sends the rich away empty
39.howItsDone: The Magnificat is sung or said every evening in Catholic vespers and in Anglican Evening Prayer, and at Lutheran vespers; Orthodox churches sing it at the morning service, with a hymn to Mary as a refrain.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two pregnant women: Mary at Elizabeth's door, and a baby who leaped. Your line was: joy knows joy. Did you reach the person who'd understand? Day thirty-nine.

We're still in Elizabeth's house, in the hills. Elizabeth has just cried out a blessing over Mary, and you might expect Mary to say something modest. Thank you. I don't know what's happening either. Instead, Luke gives her a song. Ten verses. And it isn't a lullaby. It starts with thanks, turns to her own small life, and then, without warning, it turns the whole world over. Thrones emptied. Hungry people fed. Rich people walking away with nothing. A young woman from a small village, pregnant and not yet married, singing about the powerful coming down. Churches have sung her song at daily prayer for many centuries. Today's word is its first word.
screen: `STILL IN ELIZABETH'S HOUSE.` → `NOT MODEST. A SONG.` → `THE WORLD TURNED OVER.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible it begins: "My soul doth magnify the Lord, And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour." In the old Latin Bible, the first word is Magnificat, magnifies, and that's what the song is called. To magnify is to make bigger. Not to make God bigger than God is, but to make God big in your own eyes, the way a magnifying glass makes something small easy to see. Then Mary looks at herself. She says God has noticed the low estate of his servant girl, and that from now on every generation will call her blessed. And then the song turns outward. "He hath put down the mighty from their seats, and exalted them of low degree. He hath filled the hungry with good things; and the rich he hath sent empty away." Notice the tense. She sings as if it has already happened, the way the Hebrew prophets sometimes spoke of what they were sure was coming. And it echoes an older song. In the book of Samuel, a woman named Hannah, who also waited for a child, sings something very close: God raises the poor from the dust. Mary is singing in her people's words, in the line of the women before her. Churches keep her song in different ways. Catholics sing it at evening prayer, and Anglicans at Evensong; Lutherans sing it at vespers. Orthodox Christians sing it in the morning service, with a hymn honoring Mary between the verses. Catholics and Orthodox hear it as the song of the Mother of God; many Protestants hear it as a model of praise, and a warning to anyone comfortable. All of them sing the same promise. The lowly are lifted.
screen: `MY SOUL DOTH MAGNIFY THE LORD.` · `SHE SINGS AS IF IT'S DONE.` · `HANNAH SANG IT FIRST.` · `SUNG AT EVENING AND MORNING PRAYER.` · then, large: `THE LOWLY ARE LIFTED.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and take a slow breath. Mary's song starts with thanks. So think back over the last few days and find one thing to be grateful for. A small one is fine. Someone who made room for you. A meal. A morning that went right. Now put it into one line of your own words. Not a poem. Just a sentence you'd actually say. If you have a pen or your phone, write it down. If you pray, you can offer the line as thanks. If you don't, just let it be true. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Magnificat. Latin for magnifies: the first word of Mary's song, where the mighty come down and the lowly are lifted.
Your line: the lowly are lifted. Keep your line of thanks with you today, and notice one person who's usually overlooked. Lift them a little. Day thirty-nine.

40.title: Joseph's dream (Matthew 1:18–25)
40.hook: a quiet carpenter plans to leave quietly, then a dream tells him to stay
40.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Feast of Saint Joseph on March 19, and many honor him as patron of fathers, workers and the whole Church; the Orthodox remember him as Joseph the Betrothed in the days after Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Magnificat: Mary's song, where the mighty come down. Your line was: the lowly are lifted. Did you write your line of thanks? Day forty.

Three days with Mary, all from Luke. Today, Matthew's Gospel tells the same beginning from the other side of the engagement. Joseph. A carpenter in a small town, promised to Mary. In those days an engagement was almost a marriage: ending it took a divorce. And one day he learns she's pregnant, and he knows the child isn't his. Picture him that night. Everyone in a village that size will know soon. He could make it public, and let the whole village judge her. Matthew says Joseph is a just man, and he decides on something else. He'll end it quietly. No scene, no accusations. He'll just step away. He has it all planned. Then he falls asleep.
screen: `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE STORY.` → `ENGAGED, AND SHE'S PREGNANT.` → `HE'LL LEAVE QUIETLY.`

segments.voice: Matthew says he was "minded to put her away privily." Privily means privately. It's already a kind act: he's choosing to protect her even while he's hurt. But in the night, an angel comes to him in a dream, and says, in the King James Bible: "Joseph, thou son of David, fear not to take unto thee Mary thy wife: for that which is conceived in her is of the Holy Ghost." The angel tells him the child's name will be Jesus, a name that means God saves. And Matthew adds an old line from the prophet Isaiah, about a child whose name is Emmanuel, "which being interpreted is, God with us." Matthew, like Luke, says Jesus had no human father, and he tells it through Joseph's dream. Then look at what Joseph does. "Then Joseph being raised from sleep did as the angel of the Lord had bidden him, and took unto him his wife." No argument. No speech. In fact, here's something that surprises people: Joseph never says a single word in the whole Bible. Not one line. He only listens and acts. He'll have more dreams in Matthew, and each time, he gets up and goes. He takes a child who isn't his by blood, names him, and raises him as his son. That naming mattered: it made Jesus a son of David's family line. Churches honor him in different ways. Catholics call him the patron of the whole Church and keep his feast on March nineteenth. The Orthodox remember him as Joseph the Betrothed, soon after Christmas. Many Protestants hold him up as a picture of quiet, faithful fatherhood. A man who could have walked away, and nobody would have blamed him. He stayed.
screen: `HE PLANNED TO LEAVE PRIVILY.` · `FEAR NOT TO TAKE MARY.` · `JOSEPH NEVER SAYS A WORD.` · `HE NAMES THE CHILD.` · then, large: `THE QUIET ONES MATTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let your breathing slow. Think of one kind thing you could skip today, and nobody would blame you. The dishes someone else left. The text you could leave unanswered. The call to the relative who's hard work. The extra minute with someone who's lonely. Let it come up. Don't argue with yourself. Just picture yourself doing it, quietly, without telling anyone. If you pray, you can ask for Joseph's kind of steadiness. If you don't, just let the picture settle. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Joseph's dream. A just man planning to leave quietly, told in the night: fear not. He woke up and stayed.
Your line: the quiet ones matter. Do the kind thing no one would blame you for skipping. And don't mention it. Day forty.

41.title: No room (Luke 2:1–7)
41.hook: a census, a long road, and a baby laid in an animal's feeding trough
41.carry: God arrived in a feeding trough
41.howItsDone: Many Christian homes and churches set up a nativity scene at Christmas, a custom often traced to Francis of Assisi at Greccio, and many churches read Luke 2 aloud on Christmas Eve.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joseph's dream: a just man who meant to leave quietly, and stayed. Your line was: the quiet ones matter. What kind thing did you do that nobody noticed? Day forty-one.

Luke opens the scene with an emperor. "And it came to pass in those days, that there went out a decree from Caesar Augustus, that all the world should be taxed." A census. Everyone counted, everyone registered, so everyone can be taxed. Historians still argue about exactly which census Luke means, but the effect in the story is clear. An emperor far away signs an order, and in a small town in Galilee, a carpenter has to pack up. Joseph belongs to David's family, so he goes south to Bethlehem, David's old town. A long road. And he takes Mary, who is, in the old words, great with child. No donkey is mentioned, by the way. Luke just says they went. And while they're there, the days are accomplished. The baby comes.
screen: `A DECREE FROM CAESAR AUGUSTUS.` → `A LONG ROAD SOUTH.` → `THE BABY COMES.`

segments.voice: Luke tells the birth in one sentence. In the King James Bible: "And she brought forth her firstborn son, and wrapped him in swaddling clothes, and laid him in a manger; because there was no room for them in the inn." That's all. No star in this sentence, no angels yet, no ox and no donkey. A manger is a feeding trough. The place animals eat from. Luke's Greek word is phatne. And there's a clue about the room, too. The word translated "inn" also turns up later in Luke, for the guest room where Jesus eats his last supper. So some scholars picture not a hotel with a rude innkeeper, but a crowded family house with the guest room already full, and the animals brought in at night to the lower part of the house, trough and all. Nobody knows for certain. Either way, the first bed is a feeding trough. The ox and the donkey come later, from Christians reading an old line in Isaiah: the ox knows its owner, and the donkey its master's crib. Crib, in that old English, means the manger. And near the end of his life, Bonaventure's life of him says, Francis of Assisi set up a manger with a real ox and donkey at Greccio, in Italy, so ordinary people could see it. Tradition traces the nativity scene on the mantelpiece back to that night. Christians read the manger in several ways. Some see the humility of God: the one they call the Word made flesh, laid where the animals eat. In Orthodox icons of the birth, the manger often looks like a small stone tomb, and the swaddling bands like grave cloths, a hint of how the story ends. The emperor gets the first line. The trough gets the baby.
screen: `ONE SENTENCE FOR THE BIRTH.` · `A MANGER IS A FEEDING TROUGH.` · `A FULL HOUSE, NOT A RUDE INN?` · `THE OX, THE DONKEY, AND FRANCIS.` · then, large: `GOD ARRIVED IN A FEEDING TROUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe out slowly. Think about your day as a house. Every room already full. Plans, errands, the people you expect. Now picture one small space being cleared. Not for anything planned. For whatever turns up. A stranger's question. A child who wants to show you something. A slow conversation. Keep that space open in your mind. If you pray, you can offer that empty space as a place for God. If you don't, just leave it empty, on purpose. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Manger. A feeding trough for animals, and, in Luke, the first bed Jesus had, because there was no room.
Your line: God arrived in a feeding trough. Make room for one unexpected thing today, and let it in. Day forty-one.

42.title: The shepherds (Luke 2:8–20)
42.hook: the first news goes to night-shift workers on a hillside; Mary keeps it all in her heart
42.howItsDone: Many churches read Luke 2 aloud at Christmas, and the angels' song, the Gloria in excelsis, is sung in Catholic, Anglican and Lutheran services and in the Orthodox morning service. Shepherds have a place in nativity plays and scenes around the world.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manger, and your line: God arrived in a feeding trough. What did you make room for? Five days now around Mary: an angel, a visit, a song, a dream, a trough. Six weeks on the path. Day forty-two.

Who's awake at three in the morning? Nurses. Security guards. Bakers. Truck drivers. The people who keep things running while everyone else sleeps. Now go to the hills outside Bethlehem, the same night the baby is laid in the manger. In the King James Bible: "there were in the same country shepherds abiding in the field, keeping watch over their flock by night." The night shift. Working men, awake in the dark, watching the flock. Bethlehem was David's town, and David was a shepherd once, but nobody thinks of these men as royalty. And then, Luke says, an angel stands in front of them, and the glory of the Lord shines all around, and the King James puts it plainly: they were sore afraid. Luke's good tidings go first to the night shift.
screen: `WHO'S AWAKE AT 3AM?` → `SHEPHERDS, BY NIGHT.` → `THEY WERE SORE AFRAID.`

segments.voice: The angel says: "Fear not: for, behold, I bring you good tidings of great joy, which shall be to all people." And he gives them a sign, and it's a strange one. Not a palace. Not a crown. You'll find a baby wrapped in cloths, lying in a manger. A feeding trough is the proof. Then the sky fills: a whole crowd of angels, singing. "Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men." In Latin that's Gloria in excelsis, and those words open a hymn churches still sing: Catholics at Mass, Anglicans and Lutherans in the communion service, the Orthodox in their morning service. The shepherds don't debate it. They say, let's go, and they go with haste, and find it all just as they were told. Then they tell everyone, and everyone who hears is amazed. And then Luke does something quiet. In the middle of all the noise, the angels, the running, the talking, he turns the camera to one person. "But Mary kept all these things, and pondered them in her heart." The Greek word for pondered means something like throwing together: setting things side by side and turning them over. An angel in Nazareth. Elizabeth's cry. Joseph staying. The road, the trough, and now shepherds at the door with a story about angels. She doesn't explain it. She keeps it. The shepherds go back to their sheep, Luke says, glorifying and praising God. Back to the night shift. The news went to the people who were awake, and the meaning went to the one who kept it.
screen: `GOOD TIDINGS OF GREAT JOY.` · `THE SIGN IS A FEEDING TROUGH.` · `GLORY TO GOD IN THE HIGHEST.` · `BACK TO THE NIGHT SHIFT.` · then, large: `MARY PONDERED THEM IN HER HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let the noise of the day settle. Go back over this week and find one moment you want to keep. Not the biggest. The one that stayed with you. A face, a sentence, a light through a window. Bring it back as clearly as you can. Don't explain it. Don't post it. Just turn it over, the way Mary did. If you pray, you can hold it before God. If you don't, just hold it. It's yours. Two minutes. The bell holds the time.
The shepherds. The night shift on the hillside, the first to hear, the first to run. This week's words: annunciation, Magnificat, manger.
Your line: ponder it in your heart. Keep one moment today, just for yourself. Tomorrow, two people waiting in the temple close the week of Mary and Nazareth. Day forty-two.
